facts.statement: The modern basic Katakana syllabary contains 46 standard kana representing morae, including the five vowels ア, イ, ウ, エ, and オ.
The ア-row is ア a, イ i, ウ u, エ e, and オ o; these vowel sounds anchor the organization of the Japanese kana table.
The カ-row is カ ka, キ ki, ク ku, ケ ke, and コ ko.
The サ-row is サ sa, シ shi, ス su, セ se, and ソ so; シ is read shi rather than si in standard Hepburn romanization.
The タ-row is タ ta, チ chi, ツ tsu, テ te, and ト to; チ and ツ have irregular romanized forms.
The ナ-row is ナ na, ニ ni, ヌ nu, ネ ne, and ノ no.
The ハ-row is ハ ha, ヒ hi, フ fu, ヘ he, and ホ ho; フ is commonly romanized fu rather than hu.
The マ-row is マ ma, ミ mi, ム mu, メ me, and モ mo.
The ヤ-row has ヤ ya, ユ yu, and ヨ yo; modern standard Katakana does not use standalone yi or ye kana.
The ラ-row is ラ ra, リ ri, ル ru, レ re, and ロ ro; the Japanese r sound is distinct from English r and l.
The ワ-row is ワ wa and ヲ wo; ヲ is uncommon in modern loanword spelling and is primarily encountered as the object particle written in Hiragana.
ン is the Katakana counterpart of the moraic nasal ん, and its pronunciation changes phonetically according to the following sound.
Dakuten marks transform parts of the カ, サ, タ, and ハ rows into voiced sounds: ガ, ザ, ダ, and バ rows.
The dakuten rows are ガ ga, ギ gi, グ gu, ゲ ge, ゴ go; ザ za, ジ ji, ズ zu, ゼ ze, ゾ zo; ダ da, ヂ ji, ヅ zu, デ de, ド do; and バ ba, ビ bi, ブ bu, ベ be, ボ bo.
Handakuten marks transform the ハ-row into the パ-row: パ pa, ピ pi, プ pu, ペ pe, and ポ po.
Contracted yoon sounds combine an i-row kana with small ャ, ュ, or ョ, as in キャ kya, キュ kyu, and キョ kyo.
Katakana uses extended combinations such as ティ ti, ディ di, ファ fa, フィ fi, フェ fe, フォ fo, and ウィ wi to approximate foreign-language sounds.
A small ッ represents a geminate consonant and adds a mora, as in ベッド beddo; it is not pronounced as an independent tsu syllable.
The long-vowel mark ー commonly indicates vowel length in Katakana loanwords, as in コーヒー koohii and ケーキ keeki.
Katakana is primarily used for loanwords, foreign names and places, onomatopoeia, technical terms, emphasis, and some plant or animal names; usage is context-dependent.
Katakana lookalikes such as シ and ツ, ソ and ン, and ク and ケ should be learned as contrast sets using complete words rather than isolated visual mnemonics.
Romanization is a temporary bridge; verified Japanese loanwords and sentence context are the source of truth for pronunciation, vowel length, and consonant doubling.
Katakana decoding should be tested in both directions: identify the sound from the character and reconstruct the character sequence from a spoken or romanized loanword.

relationships.description: The vowel and consonant rows organize the complete modern basic Katakana table.
Dakuten and handakuten are systematic marks that extend the basic kana inventory.
Standard yoon and foreign-sound combinations use small kana to represent contracted or non-native sound sequences.
Small ッ and ー change timing and must be practiced in complete loanwords.
Visual contrast sets and bidirectional retrieval reduce common Katakana decoding errors.
Katakana literacy develops through real loanwords, context, pronunciation verification, and reduced dependence on romanization.
